ety.text: From Middle English existence, from Old French existence, from Late Latin existentia (“existence”), from existēns, from existō, exsistō (“I am, I exist”), from ex (“out”) + sistere (“to set, place”) (related to stare (“to stand, to be stood”)), ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *stísteh₂ti, from the root *steh₂- (“stand”). Cognate with Spanish existencia, French existence, German Existenz. Displaced native Old English understandennes (literally, "understanden-ness"). Morphologically exist + -ence.

senses.d: The state of being, existing, or occurring; beinghood.
ex: In order to destroy evil, we must first acknowledge its existence.
However, with the dainty volume my quondam friend sprang into fame. At the same time he cast off the chrysalis of a commonplace existence.

senses.d: Empirical reality; the substance of the physical universe. (Dictionary of Philosophy; 1968)

ety.text: Latin exitusder. Middle English exit English exit From Middle English exit, from Latin exitus (“departure, going out; way by which one may go out, egress; (figuratively) conclusion, termination; (figuratively) death; income, revenue”), from exeō (“to depart, exit; to avoid, evade; (figuratively) to escape; of time: to expire, run out”) + -tus (suffix forming action nouns from verbs). Exeō is derived from ex- (prefix meaning ‘out, away’) + eō (“to go”) (ultimately from ). The English word is cognate with Italian esito, Portuguese êxito, Spanish éxito. Doublet of ejido and exitus.

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin exit, the third-person singular present active indicative of exeō (“to depart, exit; to avoid, evade; (figuratively) to escape; of time: to expire, run out”); see further at etymology 1 above.

senses.d: An act of going out or going away, or leaving; a departure.
ex: He made his exit at the opportune time.

senses.d: The action of an actor leaving a scene or the stage.
ex: Why do directors assume that exits and entrances need not be rehearsed?

senses.d: An opening or passage through which one can go from inside a place (such as a building, a room, or a vehicle) to the outside; an egress.
ex: emergency exit    fire exit
He was looking for the exit and got lost.

senses.d: A minor road (such as a ramp or slip road) which is used to leave a major road (such as an expressway, highway, or motorway).
ex: There are no services at the next exit.

senses.d: The act of departing from life; death.
ex: the untimely exit of a respected politician

senses.d: To go out or go away from a place or situation; to depart, to leave.
To leave a scene or depart from a stage.
ex: Desdemona exits stage left.

senses.d: To depart from life; to die.
To end or terminate (a program, subroutine, etc.)
ex: Common Lisp provides a facility for exiting from a complex process in a non-local, dynamically scoped manner.
Every ZAF program needs to call a routine like this to exit the application. Just put it in your library and be done with it.

senses.d: To depart from or leave (a place or situation).
ex: More than one-quarter (26 per cent) poor in 1991 exited poverty in 1992.

senses.d: To alight or disembark from a vehicle.
To give up the lead.
ex: West now plays a low club to the J and Q. North exits in a trump.

senses.d: Used as a stage direction for an actor: to leave the scene or stage.
ex: I take no monie, but good vvordes, raile not if I tell true, if I doe not reuenge. Farevvell. Exit Bom[bie].
